No custom types are defined in this header. The only symbol declared is the free function mitie::stem_word. std::string is a standard library type and thus out of scope for extraction.

Tokenization utility class in namespace mitie that wraps a conll_tokenizer and post-processes each produced token by replacing any digits 0-9 with '#'. Provides a default constructor and a stream-based constructor that initializes the internal conll_tokenizer with an input stream. The call operator fetches the next token from the underlying tokenizer, mutates digits to '#', and returns whether a token was produced. No destructor or copy/move semantics are custom-defined; defaults apply. Ownership: holds a conll_tokenizer member named tok. Details of conll_tokenizer are external to this header.

objects.definition: typedef std::string token_type;
objects.description: Alias type defined inside mitie::unigram_tokenizer for the token string type produced by the tokenizer. It is an alias of std::string.

Count-min sketch data structure for approximate frequency counting of arbitrary items, implemented in namespace mitie. Internally stores d hash tables (rows) of width w (columns) as a dlib::array2d<uint64>. Provides constructors to set dimensions, increment/query counts, estimate the n-th largest count, absorb another sketch with matching dimensions, and binary serialize/deserialize.

Approximate substring matcher class in namespace mitie. Stores a set of substrings using a compact CRC32-based rolling hash with a fixed-size hash table (mask 0x1FFF -> 8192 buckets). add_substring() hashes a pattern and records its bucket/id; find_substrings() scans input and reports matching bucket IDs (dlib::uint16) corresponding to stored substrings. Results are approximate due to hash collisions; capacity is effectively around 8000 substrings and later insertions can overwrite earlier ones. Serializable via dlib serialize/deserialize. Usage: construct, call add_substring() for each pattern (optionally using '*' to anchor start/end), then call find_substrings() to collect matches; use max_substring_id() for bounds.

A thread-unsafe (per instance) feature extractor that converts a word into a dense float vector using morphological substring hits and a learned transformation matrix. Constructed with an approximate_substring_set and a morph_trans matrix; exposes methods to get feature vectors and scale them. Serialization supported via friend functions. Internal mutable scratch space (hits) makes concurrent access to the same instance unsafe without locking.

A stateful feature extractor that maps a word to a dense float vector using a combination of precomputed distributional word vectors and a word_morphology_feature_extractor. It maintains a dictionary of total word vectors (distributional + morphological), scales components to unit average magnitude, and provides serialization and a 64-bit fingerprint of its state. Not thread-safe for concurrent use on the same instance due to mutable scratch space. Construction can be default (empty) or from a map of word vectors and a morphology extractor. Unknowns/OOV words produce features with an OOV indicator and morphology-only features. Details about word_morphology_feature_extractor are external to this header.

Feature extractor class for MITIE NER models. Wraps a sequence of dense float feature vectors (one per token) and exposes parameters expected by the MITIE CRF-style tagger, including window size, feature count, and flags about model behavior. get_features iterates the dense per-token vector and sets features by index with provided setter. Serialization saves/loads num_feats only. Construction is trivial; no special destruction requirements.

objects.definition: typedef std::vector<std::pair<dlib::uint32,double> > ner_sample_type;
objects.description: Alias for a sparse feature vector used to describe a candidate named-entity chunk. Each element is a feature id (uint32) and its weight (double). Acts as a container type with standard vector semantics. No special construction or destruction beyond std::vector.

A thread-unsafe (per instance) named entity recognizer wrapper around a dlib sequence_segmenter and a multiclass linear classifier. It tags tokenized text with entity spans and types. Supports loading from components, from a pair of serialized files (pure model + extractor), or from a pure model alone with extractor provided at inference time. Provides serialization, prediction, and accessors. Internal fields include tag names, feature extractor, segmenter, classifier, and fingerprinting for compatibility checks.

objects.description: Scoped enum inside mitie::named_entity_extractor indicating supported versions of the 'pure model' file format for this NER. Used to gate compatibility checks and capabilities.

Annotated token sequence used to build NER training data. Holds tokens and a set of non-overlapping entity ranges with labels; provides helpers to add and validate entities. Owned internally by ner_trainer when added for training.

Trainer that accumulates ner_training_instance data and trains a mitie::named_entity_extractor using a provided total_word_feature_extractor file. Exposes controls for beta and threading; owns internal storage of sentences, chunks, and labels. Construction requires feature extractor filename.
Container for evaluation results from evaluate_named_entity_recognizer(). Holds per-label precision/recall entries and overall precision/recall. Includes nested metrics struct for label-wise results.
Nested struct inside mitie::ner_eval_metrics representing per-label evaluation statistics: label name, precision, and recall.

Tokenizer class that reads tokens from an input stream using rules approximating the CoNLL-2003 tokenization. It splits punctuation, handles periods in abbreviations and numeric contexts, treats whitespace and UTF-8 non-breaking spaces as separators, and splits certain UTF-8 quotes and right single quotation marks into separate tokens while tracking byte offsets.

A text classification utility that predicts a single label for a tokenized text input. It owns a total_word_feature_extractor and a dlib multiclass linear decision function trained on sparse features derived from text_sample_type. Provides multiple constructors for empty, combined model+extractor, or pure model-only loading. Not thread-safe for concurrent access to the same instance due to internal mutable scratch space (as noted in comments). The class supports serialization, deserialization, prediction with or without an externally supplied feature extractor, and exposes tag-name mapping. It also defines an internal enum supported_pure_model_versions for managing model/feature extractor compatibility via fingerprints.
direct_api_constructors: mitie::text_categorizer::text_categorizer(const std::vector<std::string>&, const total_word_feature_extractor&, const dlib::multiclass_linear_decision_function<dlib::sparse_linear_kernel<text_sample_type>, unsigned long>&)

objects.description: Scoped enum inside mitie::text_categorizer that enumerates supported versions of the "pure model" format used by the classifier. Used to check compatibility between serialized decision function and the feature extractor via fingerprints.

Trainer class for building mitie::text_categorizer models from labeled text data. Manages training samples, threading, and a beta parameter controlling precision/recall trade-off. It optionally loads a total_word_feature_extractor from a file. Public API allows adding single or batch samples, configuring threads and beta, and producing a trained text_categorizer. Internals include label mapping, storage of tokenized texts, and helper training routines. Ownership: holds a total_word_feature_extractor and other data members. Construction: via the two public constructors; destruction is default. Usage: create instance, add samples, adjust beta/threads, call train().
Plain-old-data struct representing a single parsed <DOC> entry from the Gigaword corpus, capturing id, type, headline, dateline, and body text fields.

Reader for a single Gigaword XML-like file/stream. It parses <DOC> records into gigaword_document via dlib’s XML parser. Construct with no stream (acts as exhausted) or with std::istream&, then call operator()(gigaword_document&) repeatedly until false. Internal helper classes doc_handler and xml_error_handler are private implementation details.

Facade that iterates over one or more Gigaword files. Construct with a filename (const char*, std::string, dlib::file) or a vector of dlib::file, then call operator()(gigaword_document&) or operator()(std::string&) to retrieve successive documents or just their text. Manages std::ifstream and a gigaword_file_reader internally; reset() restarts iteration.

Trainer class for building mitie::binary_relation_detector models from annotated sentences. It collects positive and negative relation examples, configures training parameters (beta, threading), and produces a trained detector with train(). Requires an existing named_entity_extractor at construction. Implementation details reside elsewhere; this header only declares the interface and member layout.

functions.name: mitie_free
functions.description: Frees resources associated with any MITIE object previously allocated by the MITIE C API. Safe to call with NULL. Use this rather than free().
requirements: object is either NULL or a pointer to an object obtained from the MITIE API
Do not call free() on MITIE objects; always use mitie_free()

functions.name: mitie_load_entire_file
functions.description: Loads the entire contents of the specified file into a newly allocated NULL-terminated C string and returns it. Caller must free the returned string using mitie_free().
requirements: filename points to a valid NULL-terminated C string
On success, the returned buffer must be freed with mitie_free()
Returns NULL if the file cannot be loaded or read

functions.name: mitie_tokenize
functions.description: Tokenizes an input UTF-8 text into an array of NULL-terminated token strings. The array is NULL-terminated. Free the entire array (and contained strings) by calling mitie_free() once on the array pointer.
requirements: text points to a valid NULL-terminated C string
Returned array is NULL-terminated; e.g., {"some","text",NULL}
Caller must free the returned array with a single mitie_free() on the array pointer; do not free individual elements
Returns NULL on failure

functions.name: mitie_tokenize_file
functions.description: Reads a file and returns its tokenization, equivalent to mitie_tokenize(mitie_load_entire_file(filename)) without leaking memory. Returned array must be freed with mitie_free().
requirements: filename points to a valid NULL-terminated C string
Returned array must be freed with mitie_free() (once on the array pointer)
Returns NULL on failure

functions.name: mitie_tokenize_with_offsets
functions.signature: char** mitie_tokenize_with_offsets(const char* text, unsigned long** token_offsets);
functions.description: Tokenizes text and additionally returns character offsets of each token within the original text. Returned tokens array is NULL-terminated; token_offsets points to an array where token_offsets[i] is the starting character index of tokens[i] in text. Both arrays must be freed with mitie_free().
requirements: text points to a valid NULL-terminated C string
token_offsets is a valid pointer to an unsigned long* (output parameter)
Returned tokens array is NULL-terminated; token_offsets has the same number of entries as tokens until the terminating NULL
Caller must free both the returned char** and the allocated *token_offsets with mitie_free()
Returns NULL on failure

functions.name: mitie_load_named_entity_extractor
functions.description: Loads a serialized MITIE named entity extractor (NER) from disk and returns a handle to it. Caller must free with mitie_free().
requirements: filename points to a valid NULL-terminated C string
Return value must be freed with mitie_free()
Returns NULL if the object cannot be created/loaded

functions.signature: mitie_named_entity_extractor* mitie_load_named_entity_extractor_pure_model(const char* filename, const char* fe_filename);
functions.description: Loads a NER "pure model" saved without its feature extractor, using a provided total_word_feature_extractor file. Returns a NER handle to be freed with mitie_free().
requirements: filename points to a valid NULL-terminated C string referring to a model saved via mitie_save_named_entity_extractor_pure_model
fe_filename points to a valid NULL-terminated C string naming a total_word_feature_extractor file used when creating the NER model
Return value must be freed with mitie_free()

functions.name: mitie_check_ner_pure_model
functions.description: Checks whether a serialized NER file is a pure model (saved without feature extractor). Returns 0 if pure, non-zero otherwise.
requirements: filename points to a valid NULL-terminated C string
filename must reference a NER saved via mitie_save_named_entity_extractor_pure_model or mitie_save_named_entity_extractor

functions.description: Loads a NER pure model without also loading a feature extractor. To perform extraction, you must later supply a compatible total_word_feature_extractor to mitie_extract_entities_with_extractor(). Returns a handle to free with mitie_free().

functions.name: mitie_get_num_possible_ner_tags

idx < mitie_get_num_possible_ner_tags(ner)

functions.name: mitie_extract_binary_relation
functions.signature: mitie_binary_relation* mitie_extract_binary_relation(const mitie_named_entity_extractor* ner, char** tokens, unsigned long arg1_start, unsigned long arg1_length, unsigned long arg2_start, unsigned long arg2_length);

import os
import random
import struct
from typing import List

# Generator for arbitrary file bytes to be consumed by:
# - mitie_load_entire_file: expects any file content
# - mitie_tokenize_file: file will be tokenized as UTF-8-ish text; valid UTF-8 with
#   punctuation/quotes/whitespace gives more code paths in tokenizer
# - mitie::parse_conll_data fuzzer stub overwrites the file itself, so our content
#   doesn't matter for that stub; still keep content small and valid
#
# Strategy
# - Produce small to medium-sized UTF-8 text with a mix of:
#   - ASCII words, digits (to exercise number handling in tokenizers)
#   - Punctuation and symbols split by CoNLL rules (., !, ?, :, |, quotes, brackets)
#   - UTF-8 right single quote (E2 80 99) and unicode double quotes (E2 80 9C/9D)
#     to trigger specific split paths in mitie::conll_tokenizer
#   - Non-breaking space (C2 A0) to exercise whitespace handling
#   - Newlines and tabs
# - Vary structure with seeded randomness. Ensure total size <= 4096 bytes.

UTF8_RSQUO = b"\xE2\x80\x99"  # ’
UTF8_LDQUO = b"\xE2\x80\x9C"  # “
UTF8_RDQUO = b"\xE2\x80\x9D"  # ”
NBSP = b"\xC2\xA0"            # non-breaking space

WORDS = [
    "John", "Acme", "Corp", "lives", "in", "London", "Jane", "Doe",
    "runs", "quickly", "through", "park", "email", "contact", "version",
    "v1.2.3", "Room", "101", "Section", "A12", "appendix", "Note",
]
PUNCT = [".", ",", "!", "?", ":", "|", "[", "]", "(", ")"]

# Some tokens that include digits for unigram tokenizer to map to '#'
NUMERIC_TOKENS = [
    "12345", "2021", "Q3", "v2", "file_001", "ID-9876", "3.1415"
]

# Compose sentences using special UTF-8 quotes/apostrophes to trigger splitting
SPECIAL_PATTERNS = [
    lambda rng: UTF8_LDQUO + b"Hello" + UTF8_RDQUO,  # “Hello”
    lambda rng: b"can" + UTF8_RSQUO + b"t",          # can’t
    lambda rng: b"it" + UTF8_RSQUO + b"s",           # it’s
]


def _rand_ws(rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # mix of regular and non-breaking whitespace
    choices = [b" ", b"\t", b"\n", NBSP]
    return rng.choice(choices)


def _rand_token(rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    kind = rng.choices(
        population=["word", "num", "special", "punct"],
        weights=[0.55, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15], k=1
    )[0]
    if kind == "word":
        return rng.choice(WORDS).encode("utf-8")
    if kind == "num":
        return rng.choice(NUMERIC_TOKENS).encode("utf-8")
    if kind == "special":
        return SPECIAL_PATTERNS[rng.randrange(len(SPECIAL_PATTERNS))](rng)
    # punct
    return rng.choice(PUNCT).encode("utf-8")


def _make_paragraph(rng: random.Random, target_len: int) -> bytes:
    out = bytearray()
    # Start with a DOCSTART-like line occasionally
    if rng.random() < 0.2:
        out += b"-DOCSTART- -X- -X- O\n\n"
    # Build tokens until reaching target_len
    while len(out) < target_len:
        tok = _rand_token(rng)
        # Occasionally wrap a token in unicode quotes to trigger tokenizer paths
        if rng.random() < 0.1:
            tok = UTF8_LDQUO + tok + UTF8_RDQUO
        out += tok
        # Add whitespace after token
        out += _rand_ws(rng)
        # Occasionally add period chains like "..." which conll tokenizer treats specially
        if rng.random() < 0.08:
            out += b"." * rng.randint(2, 4)
            out += _rand_ws(rng)
        # Occasionally add abbreviation-like token to keep trailing period behavior (e.g., Jr.)
        if rng.random() < 0.05:
            abbr = rng.choice([b"Jr.", b"St.", b"Mr.", b"Dr."])
            out += abbr + _rand_ws(rng)
    # Ensure paragraph ends with newline
    if not out.endswith(b"\n"):
        out += b"\n"
    return bytes(out)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    # Decide total size budget (keep below 4096)
    total_budget = rng.randint(256, 2048)
    parts: List[bytes] = []
    # Create 1..4 paragraphs
    para_count = rng.randint(1, 4)
    # Split budget across paragraphs
    remaining = total_budget
    for i in range(para_count):
        # Allocate a chunk, leaving some for later
        if i == para_count - 1:
            tgt = remaining
        else:
            # each paragraph at least 100 bytes if possible
            min_sz = min(100, max(remaining // (para_count - i), 1))
            max_sz = max(min_sz, remaining // (para_count - i) + 50)
            tgt = rng.randint(min_sz, max_sz)
        para = _make_paragraph(rng, tgt)
        parts.append(para)
        remaining -= len(para)
        if remaining <= 0:
            break
    data = b"\n".join(parts)
    # Hard cap
    if len(data) > 4096:
        data = data[:4096]
        # ensure valid UTF-8 boundary not strictly required by consumers; but keep newline end
        if not data.endswith(b"\n"):
            data = data[:-1] + b"\n"
    return data

import io
import random
import struct
from typing import List, Tuple

# This generator produces valid MITIE/dlib serialized model files for the
# following loaders used by the fuzz stubs:
# - mitie_load_named_entity_extractor()  -> expects version 2 stream
# - mitie_load_text_categorizer()        -> expects version 2 stream
# - mitie_load_binary_relation_detector()-> expects version 1 stream
# - mitie_check_*_pure_model()           -> accept any file; we also emit minimal plausible headers
#
# We implement just enough of the dlib/mitie serialization formats to be
# accepted by their deserializers and exercise code paths. We create tiny but
# consistent models with empty/degenerate internals where allowed by the
# interfaces. All integers are little-endian as used by dlib's serialize on
# little-endian hosts. Strings and STL containers follow dlib's serialization
# conventions (versioned integers followed by container sizes and elements).
#
# Notes on formats used below (in brief approximations sufficient for fuzzing):
# - dlib::serialize(int, out) writes a 4-byte little-endian int.
# - For std::string, dlib writes a 64-bit length followed by raw bytes.
# - For std::vector<T>, dlib writes a 64-bit length then each element serialized.
# - For std::map<K,V>, dlib writes a 64-bit length then key,value pairs serialized.
# - For fundamental unsigned long/uint64, we write 8-byte little-endian.
# MITIE uses these patterns in its serialize() methods we mimic.
#
# We keep objects minimal yet coherent:
# - total_word_feature_extractor (version 2): fingerprint, non_morph_feats, dictionary map, morphology extractor
# - word_morphology_feature_extractor (version 1): approximate_substring_set + matrix<float>
# - approximate_substring_set (version 1): mask, mask_bits, init_hash, max_substr_len, hash_table, crc_table
# - named_entity_extractor (version 2): fingerprint, tag_names, total_word_feature_extractor, segmenter, df
# - text_categorizer (version 2): fingerprint, tag_names, total_word_feature_extractor, df
# - binary_relation_detector (version 1): relation_type string, tfe_fingerprint, decision function
# - For sequence_segmenter and decision functions we emit tiny valid dlib objects
#   with dimensions matching the simplest cases; we stub them as empty with
#   consistent serialized skeletons sufficient for deserialization.
#
# Important: These are minimalistic encodings geared towards acceptance by the
# official deserializers; they do not implement full model math. The goal is
# to trigger loading/exercising code paths, not to provide useful predictions.

# Helper functions to write dlib-like serialized primitives/containers.

def w_i32(buf: io.BytesIO, v: int):
    buf.write(struct.pack('<i', int(v)))

def w_u32(buf: io.BytesIO, v: int):
    buf.write(struct.pack('<I', int(v)))

def w_u64(buf: io.BytesIO, v: int):
    buf.write(struct.pack('<Q', int(v) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF))

def w_f64(buf: io.BytesIO, v: float):
    buf.write(struct.pack('<d', float(v)))

def w_f32(buf: io.BytesIO, v: float):
    buf.write(struct.pack('<f', float(v)))

def w_str(buf: io.BytesIO, s: str):
    data = s.encode('utf-8')
    w_u64(buf, len(data))
    buf.write(data)

# Serialize std::vector<T> with element writer function

def w_vec(buf: io.BytesIO, xs: List, elem_writer):
    w_u64(buf, len(xs))
    for x in xs:
        elem_writer(buf, x)

# Serialize std::map<K,V> as vector of pairs (dlib uses this approach)

def w_map(buf: io.BytesIO, items: List[Tuple], key_writer, val_writer):
    w_u64(buf, len(items))
    for k, v in items:
        key_writer(buf, k)
        val_writer(buf, v)

# Minimal dlib::matrix<float> serialization helper: dlib uses row-major bytes with
# a header: nr (long), nc (long), then nr*nc floats. We approximate with 64-bit for nr/nc.

def w_matrix_f32(buf: io.BytesIO, nr: int, nc: int, values: List[float]):
    # dlib::serialize for matrix writes versioned? In MITIE code it calls dlib::serialize directly on matrix,
    # which writes nr,nc then raw data. We'll write 64-bit longs as in other dlib code paths.
    w_i32(buf, 0)  # matrix serialization version used by dlib is often 0; keep 0
    w_u64(buf, nr)
    w_u64(buf, nc)
    # alignment: write contiguous floats
    for v in values:
        w_f32(buf, v)

# Minimal serialize for dlib linear decision function of sparse kernel used in MITIE.
# dlib writes a version then learned parameters: labels, weights, biases. We'll emit an empty model.

def w_empty_mc_linear_df(buf: io.BytesIO):
    # Version used by dlib for multiclass linear decision function typically 1
    w_i32(buf, 1)
    # number of classes
    w_u64(buf, 0)
    # labels vector (size 0)
    w_u64(buf, 0)
    # weight vectors (size 0)
    w_u64(buf, 0)
    # bias terms (size 0)
    w_u64(buf, 0)

# Minimal serialize for dlib::sequence_segmenter<ner_feature_extractor>
# MITIE serializes this via serialize(segmenter, out). A sequence_segmenter in dlib
# has a few members (df, window size, ...). We'll emit a tiny plausible object:

def w_min_sequence_segmenter(buf: io.BytesIO):
    # Use a simple version number; dlib sequence_segmenter kernel_1a_c uses version 2 commonly.
    w_i32(buf, 2)
    # underlying linear classifier for segmentation (emit empty)
    w_empty_mc_linear_df(buf)
    # window size (unsigned long)
    w_u64(buf, 3)
    # num features (unsigned long)
    w_u64(buf, 1)

# approximate_substring_set (version 1)

def w_approximate_substring_set(buf: io.BytesIO):
    w_i32(buf, 1)
    # mask, mask_bits, init_hash, max_substr_len
    w_u32(buf, 0x1FFF)
    w_u32(buf, 13)
    w_u32(buf, 0xFFFFFFFF)
    w_u32(buf, 0)
    # hash_table vector<uint16> minimal size mask+1 = 8192, but can be any size from serialize.
    # Keep small to stay within 4096 bytes: we will still be accepted because deserialize reads what we wrote.
    # Use size 0 to minimize.
    w_u64(buf, 0)  # vector size
    # crc_table vector<uint32>, size 256 typically; we can set empty to minimize.
    w_u64(buf, 0)

# word_morphology_feature_extractor (version 1)

def w_word_morph_fe(buf: io.BytesIO):
    w_i32(buf, 1)
    w_approximate_substring_set(buf)
    # morph_trans matrix<float>: we will write 0x0 matrix
    w_matrix_f32(buf, 0, 0, [])

# total_word_feature_extractor (version 2)

def w_total_word_fe(buf: io.BytesIO, have_dict: bool, rng: random.Random):
    w_i32(buf, 2)
    # fingerprint (uint64)
    w_u64(buf, rng.getrandbits(64))
    # non_morph_feats (long)
    non_morph = 1  # include OOV indicator dimension at least
    w_i32(buf, non_morph)
    # total_word_vectors: map<string, matrix<float,0,1>>; keep empty or one small entry
    if have_dict:
        def write_matrix_column(buf2: io.BytesIO, vec: List[float]):
            # dlib serializes matrix<float,0,1> same as general matrix
            w_matrix_f32(buf2, len(vec), 1, vec)
        entries = [("hello", [0.0])]  # dimension matches non_morph-1 + morph dims; we keep 1 float
        w_u64(buf, len(entries))
        for k, vec in entries:
            w_str(buf, k)
            write_matrix_column(buf, vec)
    else:
        w_u64(buf, 0)
    # morph feature extractor
    w_word_morph_fe(buf)

# ner_feature_extractor serialization: only num_feats is serialized

def w_ner_feature_extractor(buf: io.BytesIO, num_feats: int):
    w_i32(buf, num_feats)

# named_entity_extractor (version 2)

def build_named_entity_extractor(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    w_i32(buf, 2)  # version
    w_u64(buf, rng.getrandbits(64))  # fingerprint
    # tag_name_strings vector<string>
    tags = ["PERSON", "ORG"]
    w_u64(buf, len(tags))
    for t in tags:
        w_str(buf, t)
    # total_word_feature_extractor
    w_total_word_fe(buf, have_dict=False, rng=rng)
    # sequence_segmenter<ner_feature_extractor>
    # MITIE serialize() writes serialize(segmenter), which includes its own internals; we emit a minimal segmenter
    w_min_sequence_segmenter(buf)
    # multiclass_linear_decision_function over sparse kernel (df)
    w_empty_mc_linear_df(buf)
    return buf.getvalue()

# text_categorizer (version 2)

def build_text_categorizer(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed ^ 0xABCDEF)
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    w_i32(buf, 2)  # version
    w_u64(buf, rng.getrandbits(64))  # fingerprint
    # tag_name_strings
    tags = ["sports", "politics", "tech"]
    w_u64(buf, len(tags))
    for t in tags:
        w_str(buf, t)
    # total_word_feature_extractor
    w_total_word_fe(buf, have_dict=True, rng=rng)
    # decision function
    w_empty_mc_linear_df(buf)
    return buf.getvalue()

# binary_relation_detector (version 1)

def build_binary_relation_detector(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed ^ 0x12345678)
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    w_i32(buf, 1)  # version
    # relation_type string
    w_str(buf, "related_to")
    # total_word_feature_extractor fingerprint
    w_u64(buf, rng.getrandbits(64))
    # decision function
    w_empty_mc_linear_df(buf)
    return buf.getvalue()

# Pure model checkers accept any file; but they might also parse headers to decide.
# We sometimes output a short recognizable header for robustness.

def build_dummy_pure_check(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    # Write an int tag and a small string to resemble a file
    w_i32(buf, rng.randrange(0, 3))
    w_str(buf, "mitie_stub")
    return buf.getvalue()


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    # Choose which target to produce: 0=NER,1=TextCat,2=RelDet,3=Dummy
    choice = rng.randrange(0, 4)
    if choice == 0:
        data = build_named_entity_extractor(seed)
    elif choice == 1:
        data = build_text_categorizer(seed)
    elif choice == 2:
        data = build_binary_relation_detector(seed)
    else:
        data = build_dummy_pure_check(seed)

    # Ensure size limit
    if len(data) > 4096:
        # Truncate very conservatively should not happen with our minimal encoders
        data = data[:4096]
    return data

import io
import random
import struct
from typing import List, Tuple

# This generator produces a valid serialized mitie::total_word_feature_extractor file
# matching the format outlined in the headers (version == 2). It builds a tiny, but
# fully consistent extractor with:
# - non_morph_feats = 2 (1 OOV indicator + 1 dim word vector)
# - total_word_vectors map with a few words -> concatenated vector [0, word_vec(1 dim), morph_feats(2 dims)]
# - an embedded word_morphology_feature_extractor (version 1) composed of a small
#   approximate_substring_set (mask=0x1FFF, etc.) and a 2x(8192) morph_trans matrix.
#
# The resulting file is self-consistent and should successfully load via
# mitie_load_total_word_feature_extractor(), enabling subsequent fuzz stubs that
# require a feature extractor file path.

# Helpers to write dlib-serialize compatible primitives used in MITIE headers

def write_packed(out: io.BytesIO, fmt: str, *vals):
    out.write(struct.pack(fmt, *vals))


def write_string(out: io.BytesIO, s: str):
    data = s.encode('utf-8')
    write_packed(out, '<Q', len(data))
    out.write(data)


def write_vector_string(out: io.BytesIO, vec: List[str]):
    write_packed(out, '<Q', len(vec))
    for s in vec:
        write_string(out, s)


def write_map_string_to_matrix(out: io.BytesIO, items: List[Tuple[str, List[float]]]):
    # std::map serialized by dlib as: size then each pair<string, matrix>
    items_sorted = sorted(items, key=lambda x: x[0])
    write_packed(out, '<Q', len(items_sorted))
    for key, vec in items_sorted:
        write_string(out, key)
        write_dlib_matrix_float_col(out, vec)


def write_vector_uint16(out: io.BytesIO, vec: List[int]):
    write_packed(out, '<Q', len(vec))
    for v in vec:
        write_packed(out, '<H', v)


def write_vector_uint32(out: io.BytesIO, vec: List[int]):
    write_packed(out, '<Q', len(vec))
    for v in vec:
        write_packed(out, '<I', v)


def write_dlib_matrix_float(out: io.BytesIO, rows: int, cols: int, data: List[float]):
    # dlib::matrix serialization: version(int32)=3, nr(int64), nc(int64), then raw floats in row-major
    write_packed(out, '<i', 3)
    write_packed(out, '<q', rows)
    write_packed(out, '<q', cols)
    # write elements as little-endian floats
    for f in data:
        write_packed(out, '<f', float(f))


def write_dlib_matrix_float_col(out: io.BytesIO, colvec: List[float]):
    # column vector of size n x 1
    write_dlib_matrix_float(out, len(colvec), 1, colvec)


def serialize_approximate_substring_set(out: io.BytesIO, rng: random.Random):
    # friend void serialize(const approximate_substring_set& item, std::ostream& out)
    # writes: version(int32)=1; mask(uint32); mask_bits(uint32); init_hash(uint32);
    #         max_substr_len(unsigned int); hash_table(vector<uint16>); crc_table(vector<uint32>)
    write_packed(out, '<i', 1)  # version
    mask = 0x1FFF
    mask_bits = 13
    init_hash = 0xFFFFFFFF
    max_substr_len = 8

    write_packed(out, '<I', mask)
    write_packed(out, '<I', mask_bits)
    write_packed(out, '<I', init_hash)
    write_packed(out, '<I', max_substr_len)

    # hash_table has mask+1 entries
    buckets = mask + 1  # 8192
    # Fill with 0 initially, and set a few deterministic buckets to non-zero ids
    hash_table: List[int] = [0] * buckets
    # Put a couple of pseudo entries to exercise hits
    for _ in range(4):
        b = rng.randrange(buckets)
        sid = rng.randrange(0, 1 << 16)
        hash_table[b] = sid & 0xFFFF
    write_vector_uint16(out, hash_table)

    # crc_table: 256 precomputed values; we can generate the standard CRC32 table
    def crc32_table():
        tbl = []
        for i in range(256):
            temp = i
            for _ in range(8):
                if temp & 1:
                    temp = (temp >> 1) ^ 0xEDB88320
                else:
                    temp >>= 1
            tbl.append(temp & 0xFFFFFFFF)
        return tbl

    crc_tbl = crc32_table()
    write_vector_uint32(out, crc_tbl)


def serialize_word_morphology_feature_extractor(out: io.BytesIO, rng: random.Random, morph_dims: int):
    # version(int32)=1, then serialize(approximate_substring_set), then dlib::matrix<float> morph_trans
    write_packed(out, '<i', 1)
    serialize_approximate_substring_set(out, rng)

    # morph_trans is a matrix of size (rows x cols)
    # In header, get_num_dimensions() returns morph_trans.nc(), so cols == morph_dims
    # We'll create rows = max_substring_id()+1 = 8192 to be safe with hits index range.
    rows = 8192
    cols = morph_dims
    # Create a simple low-rank random matrix with small values to keep size bounded yet valid.
    # Data volume: 8192*cols floats. To keep file under 4096 bytes, we must keep cols very small.
    # 8192*2*4 bytes ≈ 65536 bytes just for this matrix, which exceeds 4KB. Therefore, we need a
    # smaller rows count that is still logically acceptable. Although the header implies hits index
    # up to max_substring_id()==hash_table.size()-1 (8191), in practice dlib will index rows by
    # hits values during feature extraction. However, MITIE doesn’t validate beyond model's own
    # expectations when deserializing. We can safely make morph_trans have few rows and keep hits
    # that land outside range from occurring by keeping substrings small and expecting usage that
    # doesn't query. For loader validity, only dimensions must be consistent. We'll set rows to a
    # small value (e.g., 64). This is acceptable for testing loaders.
    rows = 64
    data = [ (rng.random()*0.1) for _ in range(rows*cols) ]
    write_dlib_matrix_float(out, rows, cols, data)


def serialize_total_word_feature_extractor(rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    out = io.BytesIO()
    # version(int32)=2
    write_packed(out, '<i', 2)

    # fingerprint(uint64). We can compute a pseudo value; loader doesn't recompute.
    write_packed(out, '<Q', rng.getrandbits(64))

    # non_morph_feats(long) = word vector size + 1 (OOV indicator). Use 1+1=2
    non_morph_feats = 2
    write_packed(out, '<q', non_morph_feats)

    # total_word_vectors: map<string, dlib::matrix<float,0,1>>
    # Each vector is concatenation: [0, scaled_word_vec(1 dim)] then feats (morph dims) will be appended
    # by higher-level code when constructing full vectors; however, in serialized form here, MITIE stores
    # the already-joined total vectors per word. From header constructor, they do join_cols(zeros(1,1), scale*i->second), feats
    # which yields size = 1 + word_vec_dim + morph_dims. We will pick morph_dims=2 and word_vec_dim=1, so total size = 1+1+2=4.
    morph_dims = 2

    words = ["hello", "world", "Mitie", "NLP", "12345"]
    items: List[Tuple[str, List[float]]] = []

    for w in words:
        # Build a small deterministic per-word vector
        base = rng.random()*2-1
        # total vector layout: [0.0, word_vec1, morph1, morph2]
        vec = [0.0, base, base*0.5, -base*0.25]
        items.append((w, vec))

    write_map_string_to_matrix(out, items)

    # Serialize embedded word_morphology_feature_extractor
    serialize_word_morphology_feature_extractor(out, rng, morph_dims)

    return out.getvalue()


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    # Produce a valid total_word_feature_extractor blob under 4096 bytes.
    # Our construction above keeps the size modest by limiting matrix sizes.
    blob = serialize_total_word_feature_extractor(rng)
    # Ensure we respect the size cap. If slightly over (unlikely), trim from the end (still leaves a valid prefix for loader?).
    # However, trimming would corrupt the file, so instead, if it exceeds, regenerate with fewer words.
    if len(blob) > 4096:
        # fallback: fewer words
        def serialize_minimal(rng2: random.Random) -> bytes:
            out = io.BytesIO()
            write_packed(out, '<i', 2)
            write_packed(out, '<Q', rng2.getrandbits(64))
            write_packed(out, '<q', 2)
            items = [("a", [0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3])]
            write_map_string_to_matrix(out, items)
            serialize_word_morphology_feature_extractor(out, rng2, 2)
            return out.getvalue()
        blob = serialize_minimal(rng)
    return blob

import random
import string
from typing import List

# Data type: alphanumeric string used as labels/names in MITIE C API functions.
# This generator returns a bytes buffer that, when used as fuzzer initial data for
# FUZZ_PARAM_STR or FUZZ_PARAM_FILENAME sources, yields valid, interesting C-strings.
# Goals:
# - Produce plausible entity/label/relation names (letters, digits, underscores, dashes)
# - Include a variety of lengths (short, medium, longer) but <= 256 typically
# - Cover different cases (upper/lower/mixed), with namespaces and separators
# - Ensure NUL-termination is handled by fuzzer infra; here we just provide bytes
# - Keep within 4096 bytes
#
# Strategy:
# - Build a small corpus of realistic tokens (entity tags, relation names, categories)
# - Randomly compose 1..5 tokens joined by separators ("_", "-", ":", "/")
# - Sometimes include version-like suffixes and numbers
# - Ensure ASCII-only and avoid embedded NULs
# - Return as UTF-8 bytes

CORPUS_TOKENS = [
    # Common NER labels
    "PERSON", "ORG", "ORGANIZATION", "LOC", "LOCATION", "GPE", "NORP", "FAC", "EVENT", "WORK_OF_ART",
    "LAW", "LANGUAGE", "PRODUCT", "DATE", "TIME", "PERCENT", "MONEY", "QUANTITY", "ORDINAL", "CARDINAL",
    # Relation names
    "employed_by", "founded_by", "founded", "acquired_by", "acquires", "based_in", "located_in",
    "parent_of", "child_of", "spouse_of", "sibling_of", "member_of", "subsidiary_of", "headquartered_in",
    # Categories
    "sports", "politics", "business", "technology", "health", "entertainment", "science", "world",
    # Misc
    "PER", "ORG", "LOC", "MISC", "TITLE", "COMPANY", "CITY", "COUNTRY", "RIVER", "MOUNTAIN",
]

SEPARATORS = ["_", "-", ":", "/"]

ALNUM_EXTRA = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + "_-.:/"


def _rand_token(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    # 70% from corpus, 30% synthetic alnum token
    if rng.random() < 0.7:
        tok = rng.choice(CORPUS_TOKENS)
    else:
        L = rng.randint(3, 16)
        tok = ''.join(rng.choice(string.ascii_lowercase + string.digits) for _ in range(L))
        # sometimes capitalize
        if rng.random() < 0.4:
            tok = tok.capitalize()
    return tok


def _maybe_version(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    if rng.random() < 0.35:
        # styles: v1, v2_0, 2024, 1.0.3
        style = rng.randint(0, 3)
        if style == 0:
            return f"v{rng.randint(1,9)}"
        elif style == 1:
            return f"v{rng.randint(1,3)}_{rng.randint(0,9)}"
        elif style == 2:
            return str(rng.randint(1990, 2035))
        else:
            return f"{rng.randint(0,3)}.{rng.randint(0,9)}.{rng.randint(0,9)}"
    return ""


def _compose_label(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    parts: List[str] = []
    k = rng.randint(1, 5)
    for _ in range(k):
        parts.append(_rand_token(rng))
    # optionally append a version-ish suffix
    v = _maybe_version(rng)
    if v:
        parts.append(v)
    # choose a separator pattern
    sep = rng.choice(SEPARATORS)
    label = sep.join(parts)
    # random case transformations
    mode = rng.randint(0, 3)
    if mode == 1:
        label = label.upper()
    elif mode == 2:
        label = label.lower()
    # ensure length bounds (<= 256 typical). If longer, truncate at a boundary.
    if len(label) > 256:
        label = label[:256]
    # Guarantee only allowed characters
    label = ''.join(ch for ch in label if ch in ALNUM_EXTRA or ch.isalpha())
    # Ensure non-empty
    if not label:
        label = "label"
    return label


def _compose_bundle(rng: random.Random, n: int) -> bytes:
    # Create n labels separated by newlines to seed multiple FUZZ_PARAM_STR consumers.
    labels = []
    for _ in range(n):
        labels.append(_compose_label(rng))
    # Also include a few short simple labels and edge-length labels
    labels.append(rng.choice(["PER", "ORG", "LOC", "MISC"]))
    labels.append("x")
    labels.append("A" * rng.randint(8, 32))
    labels.append("name_" + str(rng.randint(0, 9999)))
    data = ("\n".join(labels)).encode("utf-8")
    # bound size
    if len(data) > 4096:
        data = data[:4096]
    return data


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    # Decide how many labels to emit; enough to cover multiple calls in a stub
    n = rng.randint(5, 20)
    return _compose_bundle(rng, n)
